title: Recall bank, Q1–33
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall bank, questions 1–33. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has recurrent infections. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Repeated splenic infarcts cause functional asplenia from early childhood, so children with HbSS are at high risk of sepsis from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus, Salmonella osteomyelitis). Protect with daily penicillin, pneumococcal (conjugate then polysaccharide), Hib and meningococcal vaccines, and urgent assessment of any fever.

questions.question: A child has fever and meningism. CSF Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci, and there is a purpuric rash. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Gram-negative diplococci in CSF = Neisseria meningitidis, often with a non-blanching purpuric rash and septic shock. Pneumococcus is a Gram-positive diplococcus, Haemophilus a Gram-negative coccobacillus, Listeria a Gram-positive rod. Give ceftriaxone, and chemoprophylaxis to close contacts.

questions.question: A child has Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis. Which statement is true?
questions.a: It is most common in teenagers
questions.b: Its incidence has fallen sharply since Hib vaccination began
questions.c: Dexamethasone has no role in Hib meningitis
questions.e: It is caused by a Gram-positive organism
questions.exp: Conjugate Hib vaccine almost eliminated Hib meningitis, which used to be common under 5 years. Dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Hib meningitis (the evidence is strongest for Hib). Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common complication, so test hearing after any bacterial meningitis.

questions.question: A child has a round, boggy, swollen lesion on the scalp with pustules, pus and hair loss. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A kerion is an intense inflammatory reaction to a fungal scalp infection (tinea capitis, often Trichophyton or Microsporum): a boggy, tender, pustular mass with hair loss and sometimes lymphadenopathy. It is often mistaken for an abscess; incision is not needed. It can scar if untreated.

questions.question: What is the treatment of a kerion?
questions.exp: Tinea capitis and kerion need systemic antifungal treatment because topical agents do not reach the hair follicle: griseofulvin for 6–8 weeks (better for Microsporum) or terbinafine for 4 weeks (better for Trichophyton). Ketoconazole or selenium shampoo reduces spread. Treat secondary infection if present.

questions.question: Which statement about retinopathy of prematurity is true?
questions.a: Stage 1 is a flat demarcation line between vascular and avascular retina
questions.b: ROP only affects babies above 32 weeks
questions.c: Stage 1 shows blood vessels growing into the vitreous
questions.d: Laser treatment is given for all stage 1 disease
questions.e: Stage 4 disease can always be fully treated with laser
questions.exp: ROP stages: 1 demarcation line, 2 ridge, 3 extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation beyond the ridge, 4 partial retinal detachment, 5 total detachment. Laser or anti-VEGF treatment is given for type 1 ROP to prevent detachment; once detached (stage 4–5), outcomes are poor despite surgery. Screening is for babies under 32 weeks or under 1501 g.

questions.question: A child has long QT syndrome. Which statement is true?
questions.b: Events occur only at rest, never with exercise
questions.c: Digoxin is the treatment of choice
questions.d: Beta-blockers such as propranolol are the main treatment
questions.exp: Congenital long QT (most often KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A) causes syncope, seizures and sudden death from torsades de pointes; triggers include exercise and swimming (LQT1), sudden noise (LQT2) and sleep (LQT3). Beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol) are first-line; avoid QT-prolonging drugs; correct HYPOkalaemia and hypomagnesaemia; ICD for high-risk patients.

questions.question: What is the most common site for intraosseous needle insertion in a child?
questions.e: Proximal tibia (anteromedial surface, 1–3 cm below the tibial tuberosity)
questions.exp: The proximal tibia is the first choice for IO access in children; alternatives are the distal femur, distal tibia above the medial malleolus, and proximal humerus. Avoid fractured bones and sites with infection. Any drug or fluid can be given by the IO route.

questions.question: Which of these is most suspicious of non-accidental injury?
questions.a: A 4-year-old with a bruise on the elbow after playing
questions.b: A 3-month-old with bruising, said to have fallen from a changing table
questions.c: A 10-year-old with grazes on the knees after cycling
questions.d: A 3-year-old with bruises on both shins
questions.e: A 2-year-old with a bruise on the forehead after a fall
questions.exp: "Those who don't cruise rarely bruise": any bruise in a non-mobile baby needs a safeguarding assessment. Bruises on bony prominences in the front (shins, forehead, knees) are common in mobile children. Worrying sites: ears, face, neck, buttocks, trunk, and bruising in patterns (hand, belt).

questions.question: An infant has a rib fracture without a clear history. What should be done?
questions.exp: Rib fractures (especially posterior) in infants are highly specific for abuse. Do a full skeletal survey (repeated after 11–14 days to show healing fractures), CT head under 1 year, an eye examination, and bloods to exclude bone disease, then refer to the child protection team.

questions.question: A child with known asthma is in distress and cannot complete sentences despite bronchodilators and steroids. What should be given?
questions.b: Intravenous theophylline as the first add-on
questions.exp: In acute severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and steroids, IV magnesium sulphate is the next step (40 mg/kg, max 2 g, over 20 minutes), before IV salbutamol or aminophylline.

questions.question: A stable child has supraventricular tachycardia on the ECG. What is the treatment after vagal manoeuvres?
questions.exp: For stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then rapid IV adenosine (100–150 micrograms/kg, increasing to 300 micrograms/kg). Synchronised DC cardioversion if unstable. Amiodarone is for refractory cases under expert guidance.

questions.question: A child's ECG shows a short PR interval and a delta wave (Wolff–Parkinson–White). Which statement is true?
questions.b: Digoxin is the best long-term treatment
questions.c: It is associated with Ebstein anomaly
questions.exp: WPW is linked to Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve (and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). It causes re-entrant SVT; atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation can be dangerous. Avoid digoxin and verapamil; catheter ablation is curative.

questions.question: The baby of a mother with lupus (anti-Ro positive) has congenital complete heart block. Which statement is true?
questions.a: A pacemaker is never needed if the baby is well
questions.b: The block is permanent, and most of these children eventually need a pacemaker
questions.d: IVIG cures the heart block after birth
questions.e: Only 20% will ever need a pacemaker
questions.exp: Congenital complete heart block from maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies is permanent (fibrosis of the conduction system). A pacemaker is needed for a low ventricular rate (under about 55/min), heart failure, wide QRS or long QT, and most children get one eventually. The rash and cytopenias of neonatal lupus resolve in months.

questions.question: A child has just been intubated. The chest does not rise well, and air entry is unequal between the two sides. What should be done?
questions.c: Check the tube position and pull it back (likely right main bronchus intubation)
questions.exp: Use DOPE for a deteriorating intubated child: Displaced tube (oesophagus or right main bronchus), Obstructed tube, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Unequal air entry right after intubation usually means the tube is too far down the right main bronchus: check the length at the lips and withdraw it, then confirm with capnography and chest X-ray.

questions.question: A child injured in a road traffic accident is hypotensive (BP 70/40) and needs sedation for intubation. Which drug is best?
questions.exp: Ketamine keeps blood pressure and airway reflexes (sympathomimetic effect), so it is the induction agent of choice in shocked or hypotensive children. Midazolam, propofol and thiopentone cause vasodilation and myocardial depression, making hypotension worse.

questions.question: Four hours after a pancreatectomy, a child develops severe abdominal pain and low blood pressure. What should be done?
questions.a: Give a fluid bolus (10–20 mL/kg) and call the surgeon urgently for possible bleeding
questions.exp: Pain with hypotension early after major abdominal surgery suggests haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Resuscitate (fluid and blood), send FBC, crossmatch and clotting, give analgesia, and get urgent surgical review for possible return to theatre.

questions.question: A ventilated child in PICU deteriorates 4 hours after resuscitation. BP is normal, capillary refill is 3–4 seconds and the hands are cold. What should be done?
questions.d: Give an intravenous fluid bolus and reassess
questions.e: No action is needed because BP is normal
questions.exp: Prolonged capillary refill and cold peripheries with a normal BP mean compensated shock; hypotension comes late in children. Give a 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess (heart rate, CRT, lactate, urine output, liver size); start inotropes if shock persists after 40–60 mL/kg.

questions.question: A child is in cardiogenic shock with a normal blood pressure but poor perfusion. Which medication improves cardiac contractility?
questions.exp: In low-output cardiogenic shock with an adequate BP, inotropes or inodilators (dobutamine, milrinone) improve contractility and reduce afterload. If hypotensive, adrenaline is used. Fluids are given cautiously in small boluses because the heart is failing. Noradrenaline raises afterload and suits warm, vasodilated shock.

questions.question: A child had hives on first eating egg and is now due for the influenza vaccine. What should be done?
questions.b: Give the vaccine only in intensive care
questions.c: Refer to an allergist to skin-test the vaccine first
questions.e: Give the influenza vaccine as normal
questions.exp: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to influenza vaccines; give it in the usual setting. Only previous anaphylaxis to the vaccine itself is a contraindication.

questions.question: A baby born at 36 weeks has been in hospital for 8 weeks. When should the first hexavalent vaccine be given?
questions.b: Only at discharge, whatever his age
questions.c: At 8 weeks after birth (chronological age), even if he is still in hospital
questions.exp: Preterm babies are vaccinated by chronological age, not corrected age, with full doses, even while still in the neonatal unit. Very preterm babies (under 28 weeks) are monitored for apnoea for 48–72 hours after the first dose.

questions.question: A preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome was put on CPAP at 4 hours and still needs oxygen at 10 days. Which of these is most likely to increase the risk of long-term lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia)?
questions.exp: BPD comes from lung injury by ventilation (volutrauma, barotrauma), oxygen toxicity, infection and inflammation in immature lungs. Strategies that reduce it: antenatal steroids, early CPAP, avoiding or shortening mechanical ventilation, less invasive surfactant, caffeine and targeted oxygen saturations.

questions.question: A 14-year-old girl exercises 2–3 hours a day and makes herself vomit after eating. Her weight has dropped slightly but is still in the normal range. She has dental erosion and calluses on the knuckles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bulimia nervosa: recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, excessive exercise), with weight usually normal or slightly reduced. Vomiting causes dental enamel erosion, parotid swelling, knuckle calluses (Russell sign) and hypokalaemic alkalosis. If she were significantly underweight, the diagnosis would be anorexia nervosa (binge–purge type). Treat with CBT for bulimia; check electrolytes and ECG.

questions.question: A newborn has rocker-bottom feet, a small jaw (micrognathia), clenched hands with overlapping fingers and a cleft palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Edwards syndrome: IUGR, small jaw, prominent occiput, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, short sternum, heart defects (VSD) and severe disability; most die in the first year. Patau syndrome has midline defects: cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, scalp defects, polydactyly and microphthalmia.

questions.question: A short boy has a systolic murmur in the second left intercostal space (pulmonary stenosis) and later has infertility from undescended testes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Noonan syndrome affects both sexes: short stature, webbed neck, pectus, pulmonary valve stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, bleeding tendency, and cryptorchidism that can cause male infertility. Turner syndrome affects only girls.

questions.question: An infant girl has agenesis of the corpus callosum, developmental delay and seizures with spikes on the EEG. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.exp: Aicardi syndrome: girls with infantile spasms, agenesis of the corpus callosum and chorioretinal lacunae, with severe developmental delay and an abnormal, often asymmetric EEG.

questions.question: A floppy newborn feeds poorly and needs tube feeding. Later he has an insatiable appetite, obesity, short stature, small hands and feet, and undescended testes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Prader–Willi syndrome (loss of paternal 15q11–13, often deletion or maternal uniparental disomy): neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, then hyperphagia and obesity from about 2–4 years, short stature, hypogonadism, small hands and feet, learning difficulties and behaviour problems. Diagnose with methylation testing; GH treatment helps.

questions.question: A child has haematuria. Urine microscopy shows normal-shaped red cells and no casts or protein. What should be done to reach a diagnosis?
questions.exp: Normal (isomorphic) red cells without casts or proteinuria suggest a non-glomerular cause in the lower tract: stones, hypercalciuria, tumours (Wilms), cysts, trauma or infection. Do an ultrasound, urine culture and urine calcium:creatinine ratio. Dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria point to glomerular disease.

questions.question: A child passes painless maroon, bloody stools. What investigation is used to find the cause?
questions.exp: Painless, large-volume dark red or maroon rectal bleeding in a young child is typical of Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates the nearby ileum. The pertechnetate scan detects the gastric mucosa. Treatment is surgical resection. ("Rule of 2s": 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of tissue, usually under 2 years.)

questions.question: How is central precocious puberty diagnosed?
questions.a: LH and FSH levels (raised, especially after GnRH stimulation), followed by brain MRI
questions.exp: Central (gonadotrophin-dependent) precocious puberty shows pubertal LH levels, rising further after GnRH stimulation, an advanced bone age and pubertal pelvic ultrasound in girls. Then do an MRI brain to look for a cause (hamartoma, tumour), especially in boys and young girls. Treat with a GnRH agonist.
